opus-5.5.text:
I think it's worth separating two questions: the ceiling of the Transformer as an *architecture*, and the ceiling of the *paradigm* we've built around it. They often get conflated.

Architecturally, the Transformer is remarkably good at one thing: it lets every token look back at every other token with almost no information loss. That "perfect memory" is a big part of why it scales so well and why it's so strong at in-context retrieval and copying. But the same property is its main structural cost. Attention is quadratic in sequence length during training, and at inference the KV cache grows linearly with context. That was fine when contexts were a few thousand tokens. Now we want models that read entire codebases, run long agentic trajectories, or reason through tens of thousands of tokens of chain-of-thought, and the memory and bandwidth costs become the bottleneck. In practice, much of the engineering effort in serving today goes toward fighting the KV cache.

The more conceptual limitation is that the Transformer doesn't really *compress* its past. It just stores everything. A recurrent model has to decide what to keep in a fixed-size state, which is a form of learning at test time. That's the direction I've been working on with linear attention and DeltaNet-style models: you can view the state update as an online learning step, where the model writes key-value associations into memory and corrects them with a delta rule. Pure recurrent models still lag on precise recall, so I don't think the answer is to throw attention away. Hybrid designs that interleave a small number of full-attention layers with many efficient recurrent layers seem like the practical sweet spot right now, and several labs are converging on something like that.

There's also a theoretical angle. Standard Transformers with bounded depth have limited expressivity on certain state-tracking problems. They struggle to natively track something like a permutation over a long sequence without leaning on chain-of-thought. Some recurrent variants, especially ones that allow negative eigenvalues or richer state transitions, can do this in principle. So I'd say the Transformer's ceiling isn't capability in the abstract, since you can buy a lot with scale and CoT, but *efficiency* of getting there.

So my honest assessment: the Transformer is not about to hit a wall in the sense of "it can't get smarter." Scaling and better data will keep pushing it. But as we move toward long-horizon reasoning and agents that live in very long contexts, the cost structure of full attention becomes the real ceiling, and that's where I expect architectural innovation to matter most over the next few years.

r001.rationale: The response says the Transformer's practical ceiling is the efficiency cost of full attention, especially for long contexts, and expects architectural innovation to matter most there.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the question of a "ceiling" needs to be split into two parts, because people often conflate them: the ceiling of the Transformer as a modeling paradigm, and the ceiling of softmax attention specifically as a computational primitive.

On the first part, I'm actually fairly bullish. The core idea of the Transformer, which is a stack of token-mixing and channel-mixing blocks trained with next-token prediction at scale, has proven remarkably robust. Every time someone declares the scaling story over, we find another axis: data quality, test-time compute, better post-training. I don't think we've hit a hard wall there, and I'd be cautious about anyone who claims to know exactly where that wall is.

On the second part, I think the ceiling is much more concrete, and it's not really about capability, it's about cost. Softmax attention is quadratic in sequence length for compute and linear for the KV cache. That was fine when contexts were a few thousand tokens. It becomes a real structural problem when you want models that reason over millions of tokens, or agents that run for hours, or anything where inference cost dominates. The KV cache in particular is the thing that keeps me up at night: it's essentially an unbounded, uncompressed memory, and you're paying for every token you've ever seen on every step.

That's where my own work sits. Linear attention, state-space models, things like Gated DeltaNet, Mamba-2, RWKV. The way I frame it is that these are not "attention killers." They are a different point in the tradeoff space: constant-size state, linear-time training with hardware-efficient chunkwise algorithms, and the price you pay is that you have to be much smarter about what the model writes into and erases from that fixed state. The delta rule is really a way of saying: don't just accumulate, actively overwrite. Honestly, a lot of the recent progress is about making the recurrence expressive enough that the compression is learned rather than lossy by default.

Where I've landed, and I think the field is converging here too, is that the realistic future is hybrid. Pure linear models still struggle on exact recall and retrieval-heavy tasks, and softmax attention is simply very good at those. So you keep a small number of full-attention layers for precise lookup, and you use linear or recurrent layers for the bulk of the sequence processing. Recent production models from several labs are already doing some version of this, which tells you the economics are pushing in that direction.

So my short answer: the Transformer paradigm doesn't have an obvious ceiling I can point to. Softmax attention does have one, and it's an efficiency ceiling rather than an intelligence ceiling. I'd also add that one of the most underrated constraints is hardware. An architecture is only as good as its best kernel. Part of why linear attention stalled for years is that the algorithms were elegant on paper but awful on GPUs, and part of why it's back is that we figured out how to make them tensor-core friendly. Any honest discussion of architectural ceilings has to include what the hardware will actually let you run.

astra-6.text:
I think we’re still far from being able to identify a hard ceiling. We have to distinguish the limits of the Transformer architecture from the limits of how we train and use it. If a model struggles with a task, is that because attention cannot represent the necessary computation, or because the training data, objective, or compute budget is insufficient? Those are different questions.

The more immediate ceiling may be efficiency. As context grows, processing it becomes expensive, and a larger context window doesn’t automatically give you reliable memory or better reasoning. There’s room to improve how models retain information, allocate computation, and learn from feedback.

So I wouldn’t say the Transformer is either exhausted or guaranteed to be the final architecture. It’s a very strong foundation. The interesting question is whether further progress comes most cheaply from scaling that foundation, changing it, or combining it with other mechanisms. A replacement needs to demonstrate a practical advantage under comparable conditions—not just look more elegant.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d separate the ceiling of the architecture from the ceiling of our current way of training it. They’re related, but they aren’t the same thing.

Transformers are very flexible. So when a model struggles with reasoning, planning, or learning from a small amount of experience, it’s hard to tell whether we’re seeing an architectural limitation or a limitation of the data, the training objective, and the amount of computation we give it. Scaling has carried us a long way, but that doesn’t establish that scaling alone will solve every remaining problem.

The practical constraints are clearer: processing long contexts is expensive, generating answers takes computation, and having information in the context doesn’t guarantee the model will use it reliably. Those constraints can become a ceiling economically before they become a ceiling theoretically.

My guess is that we’ll keep changing the system around the Transformer—adding memory, tools, retrieval, and more computation for difficult problems—and changing parts of the architecture itself. So I wouldn’t confidently say, ‘This is the ceiling.’ The useful question is: which capabilities keep improving with additional resources, and which failures persist even when we give the model the information and computation it needs? That’s where we should look for evidence of a real limit.
